title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (continued from p.177): S is a scheme of characteristic p and X/S is smooth of relative dimension n. X' = X^{(p/S)} is the Frobenius twist and F = F_{X/S}: X -> X' is the relative Frobenius, which is finite and locally free of rank p^n. The 'tilde' Cartier operator is the O_{X'}-linear map C~ : F_*(ZΩ^•_{X/S}) -> Ω^•_{X'/S}. In top degree it is a map C~ : F_*ω_{X/S} -> ω_{X'/S}.

Theorem 3 (previous page) states that this top-degree map coincides with the Grothendieck trace Tr_F of the finite flat morphism F of smooth S-schemes.

This page gives the concrete local form of Theorem 3. Let f_1,...,f_n cut out a closed subscheme Z of X, finite over S. Let f~_i be the corresponding sections on X'. Then F^*(f~_i) = f_i^p, so F^{-1}(Z~) = Z' = V(f_1^p,...,f_n^p). Functoriality of the Grothendieck residue symbol under finite maps (residue of ω over a pulled-back system equals residue of Tr ω) turns Theorem 3 into
  res[ C~ω / (f~_1,...,f~_n) ] = res[ ω / (f_1^p,...,f_n^p) ].
The residue formula and 'C = trace of Frobenius' are thus two forms of one statement.

Relative dimension 1. Because C~ is p^{-1}-linear, C~(ω/f^p) = C~(ω)/f~. The formula becomes res C~ϖ = res ϖ for ϖ = ω/f^p (the margin correction 'res C~(ω/f)' tries to fix this). If S is perfect, C is defined directly on X and one gets the classical (res Cϖ)^p = res ϖ, i.e. res Cϖ = (res ϖ)^{1/p}.

Remark 1. One can define 'Cartier-type' maps f_i : F_*Ω^i_X -> Ω^i_{X'} in every degree by duality and the trace: α ↦ (β ↦ Tr(α ∧ F^*β)), using Ω^i ≅ Hom(Ω^{n-i}, ω). But F^* : Ω^j_{X'} -> F_*Ω^j_X vanishes for j>0, since d(g^p)=0. By the projection formula, f_i = 0 for i ≠ n. Hence these maps do not recover the Cartier operator on closed forms outside top degree. Even in degree 0 the honest trace F_*O_X -> O_{X'} is zero (the extension is inseparable), whereas C(g^p) = g~.

Remark 2. The Cartier operator should also be defined on the relative dualizing module ω_{X/S} without smoothness. This works whenever formation of ω commutes with the base change F_S (for instance S perfect) and X/S is of a suitable type (lci/CM-like, locally). Define
  C := Tr_{F_{X/S}} : F_*ω_{X/S} -> ω_{X'/S} ≅ (ω_{X/S})~.
Composing with base-change identifications gives a p^{-1}-semilinear (not linear) map ω_{X/S} -> ω_{X/S}^{(p)}, which for S perfect is a p^{-1}-linear endomorphism of ω_X.

The next page applies Theorem 3 to Serre–Grothendieck duality. For proper smooth X it identifies the transpose of the Frobenius map Rf_*(E~) -> Rf_*(E^{(p)}) with the map induced by the Cartier operator on E^∨ ⊗ ω.
errors: 'si on pose ϖ = ω/f' should be ϖ = ω/f^p. C~ is p^{-1}-linear, so C~(ω/f^p) = C~ω/f~; the inserted margin correction partly addresses this.
In Remark 1, 'En particulier si i ≠ 0' should be 'i ≠ n' for the claim that f_i differs from the Cartier operator. The point also holds for i = 0, where the trace is zero but C is not.
Remark 2 leaves the hypotheses on X vague (lci/CM? equidimensional?). These are needed for ω_{X/S} to be a sheaf commuting with base change.

ideas.what: Cartier operator in top degree equals the Grothendieck trace of the relative Frobenius F_{X/S}
ideas.modern_name: Cartier operator = trace of Frobenius (duality description of C)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore from Cartier/Serre/Grothendieck duality. Standard in Mehta–Ramanathan (1985), Brion–Kumar, Kunz's books.
ideas.where_published: unsure; probably only in these Montpellier notes and in duality folklore

ideas.modern_name: Compatibility of Grothendieck residue symbol with Cartier operator (multivariable)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Curve case: Tate 1968 / Serre. Multivariable versions in Kunz's work on residues and Kähler differentials, Lipman.

ideas.what: Curve case over perfect base: (res Cϖ)^p = res ϖ
ideas.usually_credited_to: Cartier, Tate (Residues of differentials on curves, 1968), Serre

ideas.what: Trace-dual maps F_*Ω^i -> Ω^i_{X'} vanish for i ≠ n, so the Cartier operator in intermediate degrees is not a trace
ideas.modern_name: Vanishing of duality-defined Frobenius traces on Ω^i, i<n

ideas.what: Cartier operator on the relative dualizing module of non-smooth X/S, defined as the trace of relative Frobenius under base-change compatibility of ω
ideas.modern_name: Cartier map / trace of Frobenius on ω_X (Cartier modules, F-singularities)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Hartshorne–Speiser (1977), Mehta–Ramanathan (1985), Blickle–Böckle Cartier modules (2011), Schwede

missed.claim: An early (c.1972) explicit proposal to define the Cartier operator on the relative dualizing sheaf of singular (lci/CM-type) X/S as the trace of relative Frobenius, giving a p^{-1}-linear map ω_X -> ω_X. This is now the central object of Cartier-module theory and F-singularities.
missed.quote: Il y a lieu de définir aussi l'opération de Cartier sur les modules dualisants relatifs ω_{X/S}, sans hyp. de lissité, lorsque la formation de celui-ci commute au chgt. de base S→S
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical priority only. The construction is standard now (Blickle–Böckle, Schwede), and the idea that a relative version needs base-change compatibility of ω is natural. It slightly predates the usual citations.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is essentially known: C = Tr(Frobenius), its residue formulation, and Tate's res(Cω)^p = res ω. Only mildly notable is the early relative, non-smooth definition of Cartier on ω, which anticipates later Cartier-module theory but is a natural idea.
transcription_corrections: 'si on pose ϖ=ω/f' — mathematically it should be ω/f^p; the image shows a correction above.
Remark 1: 'f_*: f_*(Ω^i_{X/S}) → Ω^i_{X^{(p)}/S}' is better read 'f_i : f_*(Ω^i_{X/S}) → Ω^i_{X^{(p/S)}/S}, défini grâce à l'homom. trace (dualité)'.
'(pas linéaire, mais Λ-linéaire)' is more plausibly '(pas linéaire, mais p^{-1}-linéaire)'.
'X étant lci[?] des types[?] pour[?] tous[?] S localement' is illegible; the probable sense is a local hypothesis on X/S (e.g. Cohen–Macaulay/lci over S).
